meta.title: Check your understanding: Sun path and energy yield

objectives: Describe how latitude and season change the Sun's path, and use the noon elevation rule
Explain why the best fixed tilt is usually a little flatter than the latitude
Calculate a day's energy from peak sun hours, array size and performance ratio

questions.prompt: The rule of thumb tilts a fixed panel at the site's latitude, but for Los Angeles (34° N) the clear-sky model finds a best tilt of about 30°. Which reason does the page give?
choices: A flatter panel runs cooler and so makes more power
Summer days are longer with a higher Sun, so a flatter panel serves more of the year's energy
The low winter Sun crosses less air, so winter light is the strongest
A steeper panel sees more of the diffuse sky
questions.explain: More of the year's sunlight arrives in long, high-Sun summer days, and the low winter beam is thinned by crossing more air, so tilting steeply for winter gains less than it seems. A flatter panel also sees more of the sky, not less: flat sees all of it, vertical only half.

questions.prompt: The Sun's declination on the December solstice is about −23.44°. How high does the noon Sun stand in Los Angeles (latitude 34.05° N) that day?
questions.explain: At noon the elevation is 90° − |φ − δ| = 90° − |34.05 − (−23.44)| = 90° − 57.49° ≈ 32.5°. 57.5° is the zenith angle, measured from straight overhead, not the elevation; 79.4° is the June answer and 56.0° the equinox one.

questions.prompt: A clear June day gives flat ground in Los Angeles 8.56 kWh/m², which is 8.56 peak sun hours. What does that mean?
choices: The day delivers as much energy as 8.56 hours of full 1000 W/m² sunlight
The Sun is above the horizon for 8.56 hours
The sunlight peaks at 8.56 kW per square metre at noon
Panels run at full rated power for 8.56 hours and make nothing the rest of the day
questions.explain: Peak sun hours count energy: the day's insolation in kWh/m², which equals the hours of 1000 W/m² light that would deliver it. That June day really has more than 14 hours of daylight, mostly weaker than one sun. It is energy per square metre, not a peak power.

questions.prompt: A 4 kWp array gets 6 peak sun hours on its panels in a day, with a performance ratio of 0.8. How much energy does it deliver?
questions.explain: E = P_STC × PSH × PR = 4 × 6 × 0.8 = 19.2 kWh. Leaving out the performance ratio gives 24 kWh, which ignores losses from hot cells, wiring, the inverter and dirt; dividing by 0.8 instead of multiplying gives 30 kWh.
